title: First cars, now trains: Batteries are coming for everything
description_html:
The UK was once a pioneer of rail technology. Now, it has one of the worst electrification rates in the world and relies heavily on diesel for long-distance trains. Battery-electric trains are a solution to change the game. This week on Zero, Akshat Rathi speaks with James O’Sullivan, product director at Alstom, one of the world's biggest train companies, about a £1 billion ($1.3 billion) contract for battery-electric trains and how they can decarbonize rail travel. 

Explore further:

  • Alstom and TransPennine Express sign €1.2 billion contracts for Britain’s first mainline battery-electric trains -- press release

Zero is a production of Bloomberg Green. Our producer is Oscar Boyd. Special thanks to Sommer Saadi and Alyssa McDonald. Thoughts or suggestions? Email us at zeropod@bloomberg.net. For more coverage of climate change and solutions, visit https://www.bloomberg.com/green.

Podcasts. Radio.
News. We talk a lot about climate solutions on Zero, but after 200 episodes, we still haven't talked about trains.
This episode corrects that historical mistake.
Trains are the most efficient form of ground transportation.
With one gallon of diesel, a train can move one ton of weight 500 miles, while a heavy-duty truck would go only a third of that distance on the same amount of fuel.
Power that train with green electricity and you've got an unparalleled form of clean ground transportation.
For countries that are building out new train lines, electric trains are now a no-brainer.
But a lot of countries, like the UK, built their train networks before the age of electrification.
They now need to electrify those routes and that can be quite expensive and challenging.
This is Zero.
I am Akshat Rati.
This week, the electrification of trains.
My guest today is James O'Sullivan, product director at Alstom, one of the world's biggest train companies.
James has been leading the work on a battery electric train that will be deployed in the UK.
James, welcome to Zero.
Thank you for having me.
So this is a show where we talk a lot about climate solutions, but so far we've not had a show about trains yet.
Having done 200 episodes, I'm very excited.
So I have just recently come back from a reporting trip in China.
And the Chinese rail network is pretty impressive.
Hugely impressive. Perhaps one of the best rail networks in the world.
160,000 kilometers, 75% of it is electrified.
I grew up in India, where, again, the rail network is not as advanced, but it's pretty impressive.
It goes really in very far off places, up into the hills, down to the coast.
And now it's almost all electrified.
It's even more electrified than the Chinese network.
But for the last 18 years, this is what I call home, the UK.
And it really, coming here for the first time, felt like going backwards in time with its rail network.
You know, the UK doesn't have either the fastest trains or the most advanced trains or really even enough electric trains.
About 40% of the network is electrified.
What went wrong with the country that gave birth to the train?
I don't think anything went wrong, so to speak.
What I would say is that if we had a blank sheet of paper, we probably wouldn't have ended up where we got to today.
You have to remember in the UK, we are living off the legacy of the Victorian infrastructure that was installed at the time.
They used their best expectations, their best efforts to kind of design something that was fit for purpose.

And everything that we do now in the UK specifically is about optimizing, squeezing the last bit out of the lemon to get the best of our rolling stock when we're introducing them into the UK, compared to, say, India and China, which India is not that recent, but more recent than the UK.
China is very recent in terms of their installation of the infrastructure.
Yeah, they've had the ability to look at the UK and learn from it, I would say.
So what is it that has held the UK back from actually electrifying its rail network?

So I think there was a point in time where, particularly when diesel trains were taking over from steam trains, I mean, when diesel came in, it was seen as a revelation because steam was quite inefficient.
I mean, they're glorious to go and look at if you've got time at the weekend to just enjoy the spectacle.
But in terms of The business case for diesel, you only need one driver.
Refueling is much easier.
You can design a much simpler multiple unit to be able to carry passengers.
It was really, really effective.

Now, as we move into the 21st century, and we're a quarter of the way through it at this point, a lot of the challenges that we have around decarbonization to treat global warming, they just weren't understood at the time that diesel came in.
Some countries, particularly in Europe, decided to go down the electrification route.
In the UK, we went down the diesel route more so.
And at the time, that seemed like a sensible decision.
But only in hindsight do we realise now that actually it would have been better to go with the full electrification as much as possible.
And given you think about trains day in and day out, give us why trains are the best road transport option.
I think it's very difficult to come up with what is the best solution.
There is no one-size-fits-all.
There'll be certain things where the car has its advantages, certain things where the plane has its advantages.
Where rail has its advantage is two areas, I'd say.
One, getting into the center of a city and accessing...
Local areas, particularly if you're commuting into work, you tend to find that rail, particularly in London as well, is the closest way of getting to your office every morning.
The other thing that rail is very good at is high-density passenger movement.
Even intercity travel, you can get hundreds and hundreds of people on a single train, whereas if you're traveling by car, you'd be at four, maybe six maximum.
I don't know how many people really carpool in reality.
I suspect the average number of passengers is somewhere between one and two.
So in terms of delivering carbon neutral travel, in terms of delivering people at high throughput from one place to another, rail is probably the best in class for that.
If done right, as China has shown, you can actually make the intercity transport more Even much further distances, much more effective.
So I took a train from Shanghai to Beijing, runs at about 250 kilometers per hour, and is the faster route between two really far cities than a plane would do.

So taking in the time to go to an airport, wait for security, and get into a plane, and then land outside Beijing, then take a transport inside. whereas from Shanghai city centre to Beijing city centre, much faster.
Yeah, exactly. And the other thing about it is the comfort aspect of it.
You're not having to go up 30,000 feet into a pressurised cabin.
You can just sit there.
You can do work, connect to the internet, read a newspaper, whatever you like to do, travelling.
It all is possible with rail.

So one thing that has always annoyed me is that even though London's commuter train network is pretty good, When you take a slightly long distance train outside London, go to a city 100 kilometers away, you invariably end up on a diesel train, even though there are all these overhead lines that are electric on that same rail line.
And I've never understood why is it that, at least for the part of the rail line that is electric, the train itself isn't using that power line.
Yeah, I think, again, kind of going back to the point I was making before about the kind of introduction of diesel.
For a long period of time, it was an either-or situation.
So you have electric trains, you have diesel trains.
Some of those trains still running on our network today are 40-plus years old.
It's only recently that you've seen the emergence of buy modes where they have dual capability to run either or.
So quite often when you're experiencing that in the UK, it's because those diesel trains are a bit older and also go to destinations that have no electrification to them.
So a classic example of this would have been the West Coast mainline and out to Holyhead because that route isn't electrified.
Same with the Midland mainline. now as well.
If you go up to Derby or Nottingham, where I've come down from today, those trains were diesel, but they are introducing buy modes to replace them at the moment.
And the product you're working on now is trying to bridge that divide by adding batteries in it.
So you could have a rail line where it is not fully electrified, but because it's got batteries on board, you could essentially make that full journey electric.
Talk us through this new type of train.
So I look after our Odessia product for the UK.
It's technically a commuter train in our organisation, but we offer it all the way down to kind of metro commuter and up to regional intercity.

Most recently, we announced we'd won an order worth just over a billion pounds for TransPennine, So they will be five-car units based on our Odessia product, and they will have batteries fitted to them to do approximately, I'd say, 80 kilometres between charges.
It's really interesting, actually, that project, because we have designed the train, but we're also providing infrastructure to support it.

So where it comes off the East Coast mainline, which is fully electrified, it then does this roughly 80 kilometres range. out to Hull, out to Scarborough on the east coast of the UK, and then using Alstom charging equipment, it will recharge and then come back.
And that's effectively how you extend the existing electrification.
There could have been an option there to do full electrification from the east coast mainline to those stations.
But in the short term, the battery train is definitely quicker.
Where the batteries come in is they effectively replace the diesel battery as energy storage and capable of delivering the power to the traction system.
The challenge that we have with those batteries is clearly around the range that we can use.
And that's the same if you buy an electric car today, you kind of instinctively know that the range is going to be less than a petrol or diesel car that you buy.
But in terms of deployment, the capability is there.
And the You're not having to go to a fueling station to do that.
You can recharge either statically at rapid charging stations or dynamically under the wires as you're traveling.
So it's more of an integrated solution with the existing electrification, I would say.
Are there analyses showing that this kind of train could really help lower the cost of electrification that networks like the UK must undergo if they are to hit net zero by 2050?
I think it's not necessarily about lowering the cost of electrification.
I think there's two things that these battery trains can be, or two models that these battery trains can be applied in.
One is the one that people see, which is we deploy it on a route and it effectively extends the range of the electrification permanently.

And that's really good if you're running fairly long distances, but few trains because clearly the cost of the battery is in the trains, whereas the cost of the electrification is in the distance you have to travel.
But the other model, which is interesting because we've got a project over in Irish Rail, over in Ireland, which is relevant here, is this idea that batteries are really just a transitionary state.
So if I was to buy a new train today and I didn't have electrification, It would take me quite a while to introduce the electrification, but I have the demand now.
So for me, the comparison isn't between battery and electric trains, it's between battery and diesel trains.
And so you get that instant decarbonisation when you buy a battery train.
Over in Ireland with Irish Rail, we have a project out there at the moment where we're delivering battery trains.
Alongside that, we have a project where we're delivering a charging station up at a place called Drahida.
What the government and Irish Rail have already said, is that there is funding committed to infill that section with electrification.
So it is a transitionary state.
The battery trains help you decarbonise today, but long term, the aspiration is to fully electrify.
Where the batteries really come in is kind of playing, optimising existing legacy infrastructure and being able to extend it such that you can run off of it and come back without the need for diesel.
That's really where they excel, discontinuous electrification.
And of course, electricity in the UK is becoming cleaner and cleaner, but there is still plenty of gas in the system.
So have you run the numbers on how much carbon saving there is in this system?
Not specifically for these units, I would say.

But in general, you're talking about an industry that Again, most of the trains, whilst 40% of the infrastructure isn't electrified, most of the trains will be by nature of where we position the electrification.
They tend to be on the highest density routes.
For the trains that are remaining, again, this is really just leveraging the existing infrastructure whilst being able to decarbonize with them.
So it's not– I can't give you the numbers, but fundamentally you're taking it from what is a significant amount of output across– several trains down to effectively zero.
And when they are at the edges, having traveled there 80 kilometers on batteries, how long does it get to recharge?
It varies wildly.
I say wildly, that's probably an exaggeration, but it depends on a few things.
The main one is actually the temperature.
So if it's an average day, you'll find that the train charges very quickly because it's not spending a lot of its energy on things like air conditioning or heating.
Whereas we'd have to design the train from anywhere down to minus 25 degrees C all the way up to plus 45.
So it's quite an extreme temperature range that this is expected to be resilient in.
At the same time as well, it depends on the number of people on board.
So if you've got a really full train, you're running those things at high intensity, which can drain the energy some more.
So when we get there, it'll be about...
I'd say 18 minutes about average, but it could be quicker.
It could be slower depending on other factors at play.
And when you are building these trains, you're manufacturing them here in the UK.
But where do the batteries come from?
The batteries come from all over.
We manage a supply chain with several suppliers involved.
Really, we work with them to identify the best chemistry for a particular given route.
And depending on what the answer to that question is, we use different suppliers, but they can come from all over Europe.
There is obviously the carbon benefit you talked about.
Is there a cost benefit to the consumer as well?
Yes, there is a cost benefit because in terms of the whole lifecycle costs, and again, it depends on what you compare it with.
If you compare it with the existing electric trains, you need to think about the full system costs.
So it's not just about the train itself.
It's about the infrastructure that's needed to support it.
If you're comparing it to diesel trains, I would expect the battery trains to be cheaper to maintain, for example.
In some cases, it will be beneficial to stick with batteries for the full time.
In other cases, you might want to transition to a fully electric at some point in the future because it is the right answer.
But it is, I find, on a case-by-case basis.
Part of the challenge with electrification is the retrofit of the electrification.
One, you have to go disrupt a working railway.
And you don't necessarily know what you're going to find when you get there, so the cost can increase.

And the other is that operationally as well, you have to impact the– if you want to deliver it without impacting the services that the operator is already running, it's going to cost more for unsociable working hours, for example.
Yeah. After the break, more of my conversation with James O'Sullivan, product director at Alstom, helping build the new generation of battery electric trains.

Battery electric trains themselves are a pretty recent phenomenon compared to the history of trains. there are places in the world, Japan, Austria, Germany, that have had battery electric trains in some form deployed.
What are the markets do you think this could work in?
We see it emerging in all markets over in North America as well, which kind of haven't touched on.
UK is really, really big market though, because it's playing on the legacy of the choice to go with diesel rather than electric all those years ago.

So because it doesn't have the same level of infrastructure as, say, Germany or France when it comes to electrification, the market is certainly bigger for when it comes to battery trains in the UK than some other places around the globe.
Is there a world in which we just stop at the battery part and not really worry about the electric line to come over?
Yeah, for sure.
Again, I think this whole equation relies on how far you're taking the electrification in terms of distance and how many trains do you want to run to meet your capacity needs.
If you have a lot of passengers and you're going a short distance, chances are it makes sense to electrify because the cost of electrification will be relatively cheap.
The number of trains that you want to buy with batteries would be high, so that cost would go up.
So it would make sense to transition to full electrification at some point.
But the reverse is true as well.
For routes where you're running... with a small number of passengers over a long distance, then sticking with the battery trains might be cheaper for the long term.
Say you are to start building a rail network in a country today, and there are many countries in the world that still have to get really started on a proper rail network.
What would that rail network look like knowing the technologies we have today and the possible pathways those technologies could take?
That's an interesting question.
If you're going to do it from scratch, you'd electrify because you just do it all at once.

You'd have the land, you'd put it in at the same time as you're putting down the track, and you'd probably put the most advanced signaling system you could in as well because the first time you do something, it's much, much cheaper than if you have to come back and modify later.
In this Odesia product, the battery is spread out across the five cars.

There are some ideas where You could think of having a battery car separately from the train itself, which may be attached only at the point where you need to go via battery but be electric rest of the distance.
Are there the types of products that maybe you or your competitor that you've seen that are interesting ideas?
In trying to electrify trains a bit faster.
Yeah. I mean, the locomotive as a concept has been around for years and years and years.
So I don't think the idea in terms of attaching something that can do a duty where the standard electric train cannot is a new concept.
Is it something that I think long-term is suitable?
Probably not because in terms of– you have to remember these things are assets that need to be used time and time again.
If it's only being used for a singular niche purpose, you're not really deriving a lot of value from it.
Whereas the battery train that we've got with Odessia, we've maximized the passenger capacity.
If it weren't for the fact that we told you it was a battery train, you probably wouldn't realize as a passenger because on the inside, it looks exactly the same.
So really, really kind of playing on the existing benefits of rolling stock where we have got large amounts of capacity, not really modifying it for the sake of just having a battery train.
In 2021, at COP26, Alstom had announced that hydrogen may play a role in decarbonising the UK rail network.
Last November, Alstom has paused its hydrogen train activities in France, saying that the technology is not yet mature.
Does hydrogen have any future in trains?
I think it does.
I think, again, we have to see how it unfolds.
I mean, when it comes to Odessia Stream specifically, we've designed it to be what I'd call traction agnostic.
So again, we're playing on the fact that trains run on electricity.
They kind of don't care what fuel source is powering them as long as you can generate the electricity at the right rate for them.
So it's true of whether that's diesel, whether that's battery, whether it's hydrogen, whether it's, I don't know, nuclear fusion at some point in the future.
No, really?
No, that is a joke.
That is a joke.
But again, the point being is that we're not here to predict the future when it comes to what green technologies will emerge and power our trains.

But what we can do as integrators is design space interfaces, and engineer them in such that when they do emerge and become robust enough to be able to use in passenger operations day to day, that we're ready for them.

And today, given you're here based in the UK for this particular product, but Alstom has a global reach, where are the places that are growing the fastest, that are exciting, that are doing things that Alstom finds itself in those markets?
I think it's very easy to look abroad, but actually, even here in the UK, it's an exciting time now.
Again, the contract that we secured with TransPennine, those trains are extremely novel.
I mean, we focus on the green energy side of things, but they have other things about them that make them really, really important to the routes that they're going to run on in the future.
I mean, sustainability comes in multiple forms.
Green energy is one. but also accessibility and passenger experience and comfort.
All these things were built into the product to kind of make it a train for the 21st century and evolve what we'd learned from previous generation of rolling stock.

The other big area that's probably worth touching on is things like digitalization, where, I mean, I've just came back from Innotrans, which is the biggest rail conference in the world, based in Berlin.
And there we were showcasing our remote train operations.
So the ability to drive a train remotely from a depot whilst the train moves by itself and you've got all the cameras in place.
And yeah, it's impressive stuff.
Also the use of AI in trains as well.
How are we going to use that to improve and process the data that we receive from trains to give us more insights and diagnostics and prognostics?
So there's lots of exciting things happening in trains at the moment, I would say.
When I think about automation in driving, roads and cars are a place where unpredictability is huge and automation is more complicated.
I'm not saying there's no unpredictability on rail, but it is much lower than it would be on roads.
And of course, the cases where automatic trains have existed have existed for quite some time.
The DLR line here in London does not have a driver.
But The use case of automation hasn't been as wide as I thought it could be, given it is simplified to automate rail.
Why has that not happened?

So when you're looking at kind of automated uses in rail, particularly we have this thing called grade of automation, and it goes from one to four, depending on how unattended or independent the train is running.
Your traditional train would run at GOA1, which basically means there's a driver there.
GOA 2 is that there's a driver there, but the train controls the traction side of things and the braking.
GOA 3, which is the DLR, is quite a unique case where there isn't a driver on board, but there is an attendant to manage the doors.
And then GOA 4 is the complete unattended operation.
And what you tend to find with GOA 3 and 4 is they are on very closed networks.
So they work well in metros.
But on the mainline, it's not made that leap yet because of all the different things that interact with mainline trains, level crossings, people accessing the track.
The question has always been how do we make them safe for that environment?
But that is really the next step when it comes to the digital aspect of these trains.
Using onboard sensors like cameras and signaling equipment like the move to ETCS will start to move through those grade of automation processes. steps on the main line as well.
And one aspect of digitalization I'm assuming that has played out is on the safety side, you know, just like it has in the air infrastructure.
There are fewer and fewer accidents that happen, not to say accidents don't happen.
Here in the UK, we had a big one this year.
But how much does digitalization speed up safety?

I think it's actually a challenge there because digitalization is moving at an extremely fast pace and our ability to maintain safe systems requires that you take a slower approach and more methodical approach.
If I look at The way that we approach safety systems, it's all about reducing the probability of something happening to effectively zero.
I mean, it's so low that it shouldn't happen in the lifetime of a fleet of trains operating consistently for some of the catastrophic events.

The digital aspect of it then is how do we, for example, software-controlled trains, how do we ensure that those are– delivering functions time and time again in the same way, in a repeatable, reliable way to ensure that it's safe.
If you think about the way that AI writes software and writes code, it doesn't tend to be repeatable.
So those two things are kind of divorced from one another.
So it's not something that we shun or avoid as an industry, but it certainly is a challenge.
So you talked about the fact that this might be an exciting time for the UK rail network.
Now, The regeneration of UK Rail has been a project that's come up again and again.
There have been a few false dawns.
The most recent one now is about actually nationalizing the network, which the government has been doing for the past few years.
Are you worried that this might be another false dawn?
And if not, what gives you confidence that this time around, this regeneration, this recreation of the network, electrifying it, making it clean, actually continues at pace?

I can't speak for the wider industry, but from a personal and Alstom perspective, I think this project here gives us an opportunity to showcase the capability, not just of the industry or our products, but actually the engineers that are involved in them, the capability of the people to really kind of emphasise that when given the opportunity to deliver products, for the UK rail market.
Actually, we can take that and really show some novel products, bring benefits to passengers, make the technology greener, improve sustainability.
Because we have the capability, I think, for a period of time, it has been hidden away.
And if you read the press, most people reading the press would think that anytime I see rail in the news, it's for bad reasons.
Ticket price is going up. incidents happening, as you mentioned before.
Projects not running on time.
Projects not running on time.
So really, we want to kind of reverse that trend with this project and say, look, we have put the effort in.
We've prepared up front.
We know what we're doing with this.
Let's demonstrate it to you.
And that's why it's an exciting time, really.
It's an opportunity to rewrite the history book.
Thank you, James.
Thank you.
And thank you for listening to Xero.
Now for the sound of the week.
That is the sound of an early steam train, a sound that's been largely confined to history as trains have transitioned from steam to electricity.
If you liked this episode, please take a moment to rate and review the show on Apple Podcasts, YouTube and Spotify.
This episode was produced by Oscar Boyd.
Special thanks to Olivia Rudgard, Somersadi, and Alyssa McDonald.
I'm Akshat Rati, back soon.

So I took a train from Shanghai to Beijing, runs at about 250 kilometers per hour, and is the faster route between two really far cities than a plane would do. So taking in the time to go to an airport, wait for security, and get into a plane, and then land outside Beijing, then take a transport inside. whereas from Shanghai city centre to Beijing city centre, much faster.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, exactly. And the other thing about it is the comfort aspect of it. You're not having to go up 30,000 feet into a pressurised cabin. You can just sit there. You can do work, connect to the internet, read a newspaper, whatever you like to do, travelling. It all is possible with rail.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So one thing that has always annoyed me is that even though London's commuter train network is pretty good, When you take a slightly long distance train outside London, go to a city 100 kilometers away, you invariably end up on a diesel train, even though there are all these overhead lines that are electric on that same rail line. And I've never understood why is it that, at least for the part of the rail line that is electric, the train itself isn't using that power line.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, I think, again, kind of going back to the point I was making before about the kind of introduction of diesel. For a long period of time, it was an either-or situation. So you have electric trains, you have diesel trains. Some of those trains still running on our network today are 40-plus years old. It's only recently that you've seen the emergence of buy modes where they have dual capability to run either or.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So quite often when you're experiencing that in the UK, it's because those diesel trains are a bit older and also go to destinations that have no electrification to them. So a classic example of this would have been the West Coast mainline and out to Holyhead because that route isn't electrified. Same with the Midland mainline. now as well. If you go up to Derby or Nottingham, where I've come down from today, those trains were diesel, but they are introducing buy modes to replace them at the moment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And the product you're working on now is trying to bridge that divide by adding batteries in it. So you could have a rail line where it is not fully electrified, but because it's got batteries on board, you could essentially make that full journey electric. Talk us through this new type of train.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So I look after our Odessia product for the UK. It's technically a commuter train in our organisation, but we offer it all the way down to kind of metro commuter and up to regional intercity. Most recently, we announced we'd won an order worth just over a billion pounds for TransPennine, So they will be five-car units based on our Odessia product, and they will have batteries fitted to them to do approximately, I'd say, 80 kilometres between charges.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's really interesting, actually, that project, because we have designed the train, but we're also providing infrastructure to support it. So where it comes off the East Coast mainline, which is fully electrified, it then does this roughly 80 kilometres range. out to Hull, out to Scarborough on the east coast of the UK, and then using Alstom charging equipment, it will recharge and then come back. And that's effectively how you extend the existing electrification.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: There could have been an option there to do full electrification from the east coast mainline to those stations. But in the short term, the battery train is definitely quicker. Where the batteries come in is they effectively replace the diesel battery as energy storage and capable of delivering the power to the traction system. The challenge that we have with those batteries is clearly around the range that we can use.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And that's the same if you buy an electric car today, you kind of instinctively know that the range is going to be less than a petrol or diesel car that you buy. But in terms of deployment, the capability is there. And the You're not having to go to a fueling station to do that. You can recharge either statically at rapid charging stations or dynamically under the wires as you're traveling.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it's more of an integrated solution with the existing electrification, I would say.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Are there analyses showing that this kind of train could really help lower the cost of electrification that networks like the UK must undergo if they are to hit net zero by 2050?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think it's not necessarily about lowering the cost of electrification. I think there's two things that these battery trains can be, or two models that these battery trains can be applied in. One is the one that people see, which is we deploy it on a route and it effectively extends the range of the electrification permanently. And that's really good if you're running fairly long distances, but few trains because clearly the cost of the battery is in the trains, whereas the cost of the electrification is in the distance you have to travel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But the other model, which is interesting because we've got a project over in Irish Rail, over in Ireland, which is relevant here, is this idea that batteries are really just a transitionary state. So if I was to buy a new train today and I didn't have electrification, It would take me quite a while to introduce the electrification, but I have the demand now. So for me, the comparison isn't between battery and electric trains, it's between battery and diesel trains.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And so you get that instant decarbonisation when you buy a battery train. Over in Ireland with Irish Rail, we have a project out there at the moment where we're delivering battery trains. Alongside that, we have a project where we're delivering a charging station up at a place called Drahida. What the government and Irish Rail have already said, is that there is funding committed to infill that section with electrification.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it is a transitionary state. The battery trains help you decarbonise today, but long term, the aspiration is to fully electrify. Where the batteries really come in is kind of playing, optimising existing legacy infrastructure and being able to extend it such that you can run off of it and come back without the need for diesel. That's really where they excel, discontinuous electrification.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And of course, electricity in the UK is becoming cleaner and cleaner, but there is still plenty of gas in the system. So have you run the numbers on how much carbon saving there is in this system?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Not specifically for these units, I would say. But in general, you're talking about an industry that Again, most of the trains, whilst 40% of the infrastructure isn't electrified, most of the trains will be by nature of where we position the electrification. They tend to be on the highest density routes. For the trains that are remaining, again, this is really just leveraging the existing infrastructure whilst being able to decarbonize with them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it's not– I can't give you the numbers, but fundamentally you're taking it from what is a significant amount of output across– several trains down to effectively zero.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And when they are at the edges, having traveled there 80 kilometers on batteries, how long does it get to recharge?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It varies wildly. I say wildly, that's probably an exaggeration, but it depends on a few things. The main one is actually the temperature. So if it's an average day, you'll find that the train charges very quickly because it's not spending a lot of its energy on things like air conditioning or heating. Whereas we'd have to design the train from anywhere down to minus 25 degrees C all the way up to plus 45.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it's quite an extreme temperature range that this is expected to be resilient in. At the same time as well, it depends on the number of people on board. So if you've got a really full train, you're running those things at high intensity, which can drain the energy some more. So when we get there, it'll be about... I'd say 18 minutes about average, but it could be quicker.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It could be slower depending on other factors at play.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And when you are building these trains, you're manufacturing them here in the UK. But where do the batteries come from?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The batteries come from all over. We manage a supply chain with several suppliers involved. Really, we work with them to identify the best chemistry for a particular given route. And depending on what the answer to that question is, we use different suppliers, but they can come from all over Europe.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is obviously the carbon benefit you talked about. Is there a cost benefit to the consumer as well?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yes, there is a cost benefit because in terms of the whole lifecycle costs, and again, it depends on what you compare it with. If you compare it with the existing electric trains, you need to think about the full system costs. So it's not just about the train itself. It's about the infrastructure that's needed to support it. If you're comparing it to diesel trains, I would expect the battery trains to be cheaper to maintain, for example.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In some cases, it will be beneficial to stick with batteries for the full time. In other cases, you might want to transition to a fully electric at some point in the future because it is the right answer. But it is, I find, on a case-by-case basis. Part of the challenge with electrification is the retrofit of the electrification. One, you have to go disrupt a working railway. And you don't necessarily know what you're going to find when you get there, so the cost can increase.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the other is that operationally as well, you have to impact the– if you want to deliver it without impacting the services that the operator is already running, it's going to cost more for unsociable working hours, for example.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah. After the break, more of my conversation with James O'Sullivan, product director at Alstom, helping build the new generation of battery electric trains. Battery electric trains themselves are a pretty recent phenomenon compared to the history of trains. there are places in the world, Japan, Austria, Germany, that have had battery electric trains in some form deployed. What are the markets do you think this could work in?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We see it emerging in all markets over in North America as well, which kind of haven't touched on. UK is really, really big market though, because it's playing on the legacy of the choice to go with diesel rather than electric all those years ago. So because it doesn't have the same level of infrastructure as, say, Germany or France when it comes to electrification, the market is certainly bigger for when it comes to battery trains in the UK than some other places around the globe.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is there a world in which we just stop at the battery part and not really worry about the electric line to come over?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, for sure. Again, I think this whole equation relies on how far you're taking the electrification in terms of distance and how many trains do you want to run to meet your capacity needs. If you have a lot of passengers and you're going a short distance, chances are it makes sense to electrify because the cost of electrification will be relatively cheap. The number of trains that you want to buy with batteries would be high, so that cost would go up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it would make sense to transition to full electrification at some point. But the reverse is true as well. For routes where you're running... with a small number of passengers over a long distance, then sticking with the battery trains might be cheaper for the long term.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Say you are to start building a rail network in a country today, and there are many countries in the world that still have to get really started on a proper rail network. What would that rail network look like knowing the technologies we have today and the possible pathways those technologies could take?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's an interesting question. If you're going to do it from scratch, you'd electrify because you just do it all at once. You'd have the land, you'd put it in at the same time as you're putting down the track, and you'd probably put the most advanced signaling system you could in as well because the first time you do something, it's much, much cheaper than if you have to come back and modify later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In this Odesia product, the battery is spread out across the five cars. There are some ideas where You could think of having a battery car separately from the train itself, which may be attached only at the point where you need to go via battery but be electric rest of the distance. Are there the types of products that maybe you or your competitor that you've seen that are interesting ideas?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In trying to electrify trains a bit faster.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, the locomotive as a concept has been around for years and years and years. So I don't think the idea in terms of attaching something that can do a duty where the standard electric train cannot is a new concept. Is it something that I think long-term is suitable? Probably not because in terms of– you have to remember these things are assets that need to be used time and time again.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If it's only being used for a singular niche purpose, you're not really deriving a lot of value from it. Whereas the battery train that we've got with Odessia, we've maximized the passenger capacity. If it weren't for the fact that we told you it was a battery train, you probably wouldn't realize as a passenger because on the inside, it looks exactly the same. So really, really kind of playing on the existing benefits of rolling stock where we have got large amounts of capacity, not really modifying it for the sake of just having a battery train.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In 2021, at COP26, Alstom had announced that hydrogen may play a role in decarbonising the UK rail network. Last November, Alstom has paused its hydrogen train activities in France, saying that the technology is not yet mature. Does hydrogen have any future in trains?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think it does. I think, again, we have to see how it unfolds. I mean, when it comes to Odessia Stream specifically, we've designed it to be what I'd call traction agnostic. So again, we're playing on the fact that trains run on electricity. They kind of don't care what fuel source is powering them as long as you can generate the electricity at the right rate for them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it's true of whether that's diesel, whether that's battery, whether it's hydrogen, whether it's, I don't know, nuclear fusion at some point in the future.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: No, really?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No, that is a joke. That is a joke. But again, the point being is that we're not here to predict the future when it comes to what green technologies will emerge and power our trains. But what we can do as integrators is design space interfaces, and engineer them in such that when they do emerge and become robust enough to be able to use in passenger operations day to day, that we're ready for them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And today, given you're here based in the UK for this particular product, but Alstom has a global reach, where are the places that are growing the fastest, that are exciting, that are doing things that Alstom finds itself in those markets?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think it's very easy to look abroad, but actually, even here in the UK, it's an exciting time now. Again, the contract that we secured with TransPennine, those trains are extremely novel. I mean, we focus on the green energy side of things, but they have other things about them that make them really, really important to the routes that they're going to run on in the future. I mean, sustainability comes in multiple forms.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Green energy is one. but also accessibility and passenger experience and comfort. All these things were built into the product to kind of make it a train for the 21st century and evolve what we'd learned from previous generation of rolling stock. The other big area that's probably worth touching on is things like digitalization, where, I mean, I've just came back from Innotrans, which is the biggest rail conference in the world, based in Berlin.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And there we were showcasing our remote train operations. So the ability to drive a train remotely from a depot whilst the train moves by itself and you've got all the cameras in place. And yeah, it's impressive stuff. Also the use of AI in trains as well. How are we going to use that to improve and process the data that we receive from trains to give us more insights and diagnostics and prognostics?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So there's lots of exciting things happening in trains at the moment, I would say.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: When I think about automation in driving, roads and cars are a place where unpredictability is huge and automation is more complicated. I'm not saying there's no unpredictability on rail, but it is much lower than it would be on roads. And of course, the cases where automatic trains have existed have existed for quite some time. The DLR line here in London does not have a driver. But The use case of automation hasn't been as wide as I thought it could be, given it is simplified to automate rail.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Why has that not happened?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So when you're looking at kind of automated uses in rail, particularly we have this thing called grade of automation, and it goes from one to four, depending on how unattended or independent the train is running. Your traditional train would run at GOA1, which basically means there's a driver there. GOA 2 is that there's a driver there, but the train controls the traction side of things and the braking.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: GOA 3, which is the DLR, is quite a unique case where there isn't a driver on board, but there is an attendant to manage the doors. And then GOA 4 is the complete unattended operation. And what you tend to find with GOA 3 and 4 is they are on very closed networks. So they work well in metros. But on the mainline, it's not made that leap yet because of all the different things that interact with mainline trains, level crossings, people accessing the track.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The question has always been how do we make them safe for that environment? But that is really the next step when it comes to the digital aspect of these trains. Using onboard sensors like cameras and signaling equipment like the move to ETCS will start to move through those grade of automation processes. steps on the main line as well.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And one aspect of digitalization I'm assuming that has played out is on the safety side, you know, just like it has in the air infrastructure. There are fewer and fewer accidents that happen, not to say accidents don't happen. Here in the UK, we had a big one this year. But how much does digitalization speed up safety?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think it's actually a challenge there because digitalization is moving at an extremely fast pace and our ability to maintain safe systems requires that you take a slower approach and more methodical approach. If I look at The way that we approach safety systems, it's all about reducing the probability of something happening to effectively zero. I mean, it's so low that it shouldn't happen in the lifetime of a fleet of trains operating consistently for some of the catastrophic events.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The digital aspect of it then is how do we, for example, software-controlled trains, how do we ensure that those are– delivering functions time and time again in the same way, in a repeatable, reliable way to ensure that it's safe. If you think about the way that AI writes software and writes code, it doesn't tend to be repeatable. So those two things are kind of divorced from one another.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it's not something that we shun or avoid as an industry, but it certainly is a challenge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So you talked about the fact that this might be an exciting time for the UK rail network. Now, The regeneration of UK Rail has been a project that's come up again and again. There have been a few false dawns. The most recent one now is about actually nationalizing the network, which the government has been doing for the past few years. Are you worried that this might be another false dawn?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And if not, what gives you confidence that this time around, this regeneration, this recreation of the network, electrifying it, making it clean, actually continues at pace?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I can't speak for the wider industry, but from a personal and Alstom perspective, I think this project here gives us an opportunity to showcase the capability, not just of the industry or our products, but actually the engineers that are involved in them, the capability of the people to really kind of emphasise that when given the opportunity to deliver products, for the UK rail market. Actually, we can take that and really show some novel products, bring benefits to passengers, make the technology greener, improve sustainability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Because we have the capability, I think, for a period of time, it has been hidden away. And if you read the press, most people reading the press would think that anytime I see rail in the news, it's for bad reasons. Ticket price is going up. incidents happening, as you mentioned before.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Projects not running on time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Projects not running on time. So really, we want to kind of reverse that trend with this project and say, look, we have put the effort in. We've prepared up front. We know what we're doing with this. Let's demonstrate it to you. And that's why it's an exciting time, really. It's an opportunity to rewrite the history book.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you, James.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And thank you for listening to Xero. Now for the sound of the week. That is the sound of an early steam train, a sound that's been largely confined to history as trains have transitioned from steam to electricity. If you liked this episode, please take a moment to rate and review the show on Apple Podcasts, YouTube and Spotify. This episode was produced by Oscar Boyd. Special thanks to Olivia Rudgard, Somersadi, and Alyssa McDonald.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'm Akshat Rati, back soon.

study.one_liner_ko: Alstom의 제품 디렉터가 영국의 디젤 의존 철도를 배터리 전기열차로 어떻게 탈탄소화할 수 있는지, 그리고 그 경제성과 한계를 설명한다.
summary_ko: 영국은 철도의 발상지지만 전철화율이 약 40%에 그치고 장거리 노선은 디젤에 의존한다. 빅토리아 시대 인프라를 물려받았고, 디젤이 더 합리적으로 보이던 시절의 선택이 지금까지 이어진 결과라고 게스트는 설명한다.
Alstom은 TransPennine Express용으로 약 10억 파운드 규모의 배터리 전기열차(Odessia 기반, 5량 편성)를 수주했다. 전철화 구간에서 벗어나 약 80km를 배터리로 달리고, 종착역 충전 설비로 재충전한 뒤 돌아온다.
배터리 열차는 두 가지 모델로 쓰인다. 하나는 승객은 적고 거리가 긴 노선에서 영구적으로 전철화를 보완하는 것이고, 다른 하나는 완전 전철화 전까지의 과도기 해법이다. 비교 대상은 전기열차가 아니라 디젤열차라는 점이 핵심이다.
충전 시간은 평균 약 18분이지만 기온과 승객 수에 따라 달라진다. 노선마다 총비용을 따져 전철화 확대와 배터리 유지 중 하나를 고르는 사례별 접근이 필요하다.
수소는 여전히 가능성이 있다고 보지만, Odessia는 동력원에 구애받지 않는 설계(traction agnostic)다. 원격 운행, AI, 자동화 등장도 논의되지만, 안전 인증은 속도가 느리고 신중해야 해서 디지털화와 긴장 관계가 있다.
영국 철도 재건은 이전에도 헛된 희망으로 끝난 적이 있다. 게스트는 이번 프로젝트가 기술과 엔지니어의 역량을 보여주고 부정적인 철도 뉴스의 흐름을 뒤집을 기회라고 말한다.
study.summary_en: This week's Zero is about trains, finally. The host talks to James O'Sullivan from Alstom about the UK's rail network, which is only about 40% electrified because it inherited Victorian infrastructure and chose diesel decades ago. Alstom just won a billion-pound order for battery trains that run about 80 kilometres off the wires and recharge at the end of the line. James's point is that the real comparison is battery versus diesel, not battery versus electric. Sometimes batteries are a stopgap before full electrification, and sometimes they're the cheaper long-term answer. He also touched on hydrogen, automation and AI, and said this project is a chance to change the story about UK rail.

expressions.nuance_ko: 결정이 너무 명백할 때 쓰는 구어체다. 회의에서 'It's a no-brainer'로 의견을 강하게 밀 때 좋다. 상대의 선택에 쓰면 무례하게 들릴 수 있다.
examples: At that price, the upgrade is a no-brainer.
Taking the direct flight was a no-brainer, even if it cost more.
For a free trial with no commitment, it's a no-brainer.

similar.example: The case for hiring her is a slam dunk.
Honestly, that was an easy call.

expressions.nuance_ko: 'best'를 묻는 질문에 단정하지 않고 맥락 의존성을 강조할 때 쓰는 안전하고 세련된 답변이다. 패널 토론에서 질문을 한 번 받아넘길 때 유용하다.
examples: When it comes to remote work, there's no one-size-fits-all.
There's no one-size-fits-all diet; it depends on your body.
I don't believe in one-size-fits-all management styles.

similar.example: Honestly, it depends on the context.
Different tools for different jobs: horses for courses.

expressions.quote: rail is probably the best in class for that
expressions.nuance_ko: 제품, 서비스, 인물을 평가할 때 쓰는 비즈니스 표현이다. 'probably'를 붙여 단정을 누그러뜨린 점도 참고할 만하다. 하이픈을 붙여 형용사로도 쓴다(best-in-class service).
examples: Their customer support is best in class.
That hotel's gym is best in class for the price.
We want best-in-class tools, not just good enough ones.

similar.example: Their service is second to none.
It's a top-of-the-line model.

expressions.quote: only in hindsight do we realise now that actually it would have been better
expressions.nuance_ko: 과거 결정이 당시엔 합리적이었음을 인정하면서 지금은 다르게 본다고 말하는 방어적·성찰적 표현이다. 'only in hindsight do we…'처럼 부정 부사가 앞에 오면 주어·동사가 도치된다.
examples: Only in hindsight did I see how stressed he was.
It seemed like a great deal; only in hindsight was it clearly a mistake.
Only in hindsight do you realize how much that move changed things.

similar.example: With the benefit of hindsight, I'd have left earlier.
Looking back, it was an obvious warning sign.

expressions.quote: decided to go down the electrification route
expressions.nuance_ko: 여러 선택지 중 한 가지 노선을 택했다고 말할 때 쓴다. 'go down the X route'에는 한번 택하면 되돌리기 어려운 길이라는 뉘앙스가 있다. 'go the ... route'도 같은 뜻이다.
examples: We decided to go down the cheaper route and rent instead of buy.
If you go down the legal route, expect it to take months.
Many cities went down the car-centric route in the 1960s.

similar.example: We opted for the early flight.
Let's take a more cautious approach.

expressions.quote: But it is, I find, on a case-by-case basis.
expressions.nuance_ko: 일률적 규칙이 없고 개별 상황을 보고 판단한다는 뜻이다. 정책, 예외 승인, 협상 답변에서 입장을 열어두기에 좋다. 어떤 기준으로 판단하는지는 따로 설명해야 설득력이 있다.
examples: We handle refund requests on a case-by-case basis.
Exceptions to the dress code are made on a case-by-case basis.
I'd look at those offers on a case-by-case basis.

similar.example: It could go either way, depending on the circumstances.

similar.expression: judge each case on its merits
similar.example: We judge each application on its merits.

expressions.expression: the comparison isn't between X and Y, it's between X and Z
expressions.quote: the comparison isn't between battery and electric trains, it's between battery and diesel trains
expressions.meaning_ko: 비교 대상은 X와 Y가 아니라 X와 Z다 (비교 기준 재설정)
expressions.nuance_ko: 상대가 잘못된 기준으로 비교한다고 느낄 때 논점을 프레임 전환하는 강력한 토론 패턴이다. 'The real question isn't A, it's B'와 같은 구조다. 반박할 때 정중하게 프레임을 바꿀 수 있다.
examples: For me, the comparison isn't between this job and my old one, it's between this job and staying unemployed.
The comparison isn't between flying and driving, it's between flying and not going at all.
The comparison isn't between our price and theirs, it's between paying and doing it ourselves.

similar.expression: the real question isn't X, it's Y
similar.example: The real question isn't whether we can, it's whether we should.

similar.expression: it's not so much X as Y
similar.example: It's not so much the cost as the hassle.

expressions.nuance_ko: 동사 leverage는 비즈니스 구어에서 'use'보다 전략적인 느낌으로 쓴다. 남용하면 상투적으로 들릴 수 있으니 가진 것을 최대한 활용한다는 맥락에 맞춰 쓰자.
examples: We can leverage our existing customer base to launch the new app.
She leveraged her network to land the interview.
Let's leverage what we already have instead of buying new software.

similar.example: We can build on last year's success.
They capitalised on the timing.

expressions.expression: It varies wildly. I say wildly, that's probably an exaggeration
expressions.quote: It varies wildly. I say wildly, that's probably an exaggeration
expressions.nuance_ko: 과한 표현을 쓴 뒤 곧바로 스스로 보정해 정확하고 신중한 인상을 준다. 전문가가 수치나 강도를 정밀하게 다루는 말투다. 'I say X, that's probably an exaggeration' 틀로 재사용할 수 있다.
examples: It's a disaster. Well, disaster is probably an exaggeration, but it's not good.
He's furious. I say furious, that's too strong, but he's definitely annoyed.
Prices have collapsed. I say collapsed, that's an overstatement, but they've dropped a lot.

similar.example: We're broke. Well, that's probably overstating it.
To be fair, it's not that bad.

expressions.expression: the reverse is true as well
expressions.quote: But the reverse is true as well.
expressions.nuance_ko: 앞서 한 논리의 반대 조건에서도 결론이 대칭적으로 성립함을 보여준다. 논증을 균형 있게 마무리하는 데 좋다. 'The converse is also true'는 더 격식 있다.
examples: A strong dollar hurts exporters, but the reverse is true as well for importers.
Big teams are slower to decide, but the reverse is true as well: small teams miss things.
Cheap flights are tempting, but the reverse is true as well; a good deal can cost you time.

similar.example: He trusts her and vice versa.
The same goes for the other option.

expressions.quote: There have been a few false dawns
expressions.meaning_ko: 희망을 줬다가 결국 무산된 헛된 전망
expressions.nuance_ko: 경제·정치 뉴스에서 자주 쓰이는 표현이다. 반복된 실패 뒤에 '이번에도 그럴까?'라고 회의를 표할 때 쓴다. 'Is this another false dawn?' 형태로 자주 나온다.
examples: The market rally last spring turned out to be a false dawn.
After two false dawns, I'm cautious about the new product.
Is this peace deal real, or just another false dawn?

similar.example: That clue turned out to be a red herring.
The announcement raised false hopes.

expressions.quote: an opportunity to rewrite the history book
expressions.nuance_ko: 과거의 평가나 판세를 뒤집을 만한 성과를 말할 때 쓴다. 보통 복수형 'the history books'로 쓰고 스포츠·정치에서도 흔하다. 다소 극적인 어조다.
examples: If we win tonight, we'll rewrite the history books.
She's hoping to rewrite the history books with this discovery.
This startup wants to rewrite the history books on electric flight.

similar.example: They made history with that win.
We need to change the narrative around this brand.

expressions.quote: not really modifying it for the sake of just having a battery train
expressions.nuance_ko: 'for the sake of X'는 실질적 목적 없이 그것 자체를 위해 하는 행동을 비판적으로 말할 때 자주 쓴다. 'not X for the sake of X' 형태가 가장 흔하다. 회의에서 불필요한 변경을 막을 때도 쓸 수 있다.
examples: I don't want to change the process for the sake of change.
Let's not add features for the sake of having more features.
He argues for the sake of arguing.

similar.example: The meeting was purely for show.

similar.expression: just for the sake of it
similar.example: I don't do it just for the sake of it.

expressions.quote: it's not made that leap yet
expressions.nuance_ko: 기술이나 사업이 한 영역에서 다음 영역으로 넘어가는 큰 전환을 말한다. 'It hasn't made the leap to...'처럼 아직 전환하지 못했다는 부정문에서 자주 쓴다. 이 대화에서는 비격식 구어의 'it's not made'가 사용됐다.
examples: Self-driving cars still haven't made the leap from testing to everyday use.
He made the leap from engineering to management last year.
Will podcasts make the leap to video for good?

similar.example: I finally took the plunge and quit my job.
Her music crossed over to a wider audience.

expressions.quote: given you think about trains day in and day out
expressions.nuance_ko: 누군가가 해당 주제를 늘 다루는 전문가임을 강조하며 질문을 던질 때 좋다. 반복적이거나 힘든 일상을 묘사할 때도 쓴다. 격식 없는 중립적 표현이다.
examples: You deal with customers day in and day out, so what's your take?
She practices piano day in and day out.
Doing the same commute day in and day out wears you down.

similar.example: It rained day after day.
They worked around the clock.

vocab.example: The railway is spending a lot to replace its ageing rolling stock.
We're still struggling with legacy software from the 1990s.
They retrofitted the old building with solar panels.
The new checkout system doubled our throughput at peak hours.
The team proved resilient after losing its biggest client.
Our app is platform agnostic, so it runs on any phone.
She came up with a novel way to cut meeting time.
The city plans to infill empty lots with affordable housing.
He's very methodical about planning every trip.
Please don't leave your bags unattended at the airport.
It's a niche product, but it has a loyal following.
The fireworks over the harbour were quite a spectacle.
Many investors shun risky markets when rates rise.
Predictive maintenance relies on diagnostics and prognostics from sensor data.

warmup.q: How do you usually travel between cities, and what makes you choose train, plane or car?
warmup.hint_ko: 소요 시간, 도심 접근성, 편의성, 비용, 일하며 이동할 수 있는지 등을 비교해 보자.

warmup.q: Which country's public transport impressed you most, and why?
warmup.hint_ko: 구체적인 경험(정시성, 요금, 환승)과 그 나라의 인프라 역사를 연결해 말해 보자.

opinion.q: James says there's no one-size-fits-all solution for transport. Do you agree, or do you think governments should pick one winner?
opinion.hint_ko: 지역 특성, 인구 밀도, 거리, 예산 제약을 근거로 들고, 선택과 집중의 장단점도 비교해 보자.

opinion.q: Why do old systems like legacy infrastructure stick around so long, and how should a country decide when to rebuild versus patch?
opinion.hint_ko: 매몰비용, 정치 일정, 중단 비용, 점진 개선의 이점 등을 짚어 보자. 개인 경험(회사 시스템 등)도 좋다.

debate.q: Should countries with partial electrification prioritise battery trains over completing full electrification?
debate.for: 배터리 열차는 도입이 빠르고 즉시 디젤을 대체한다. 노선이 길고 승객이 적은 구간에서는 전철화보다 총비용이 낮을 수 있으며, 기존 인프라도 활용할 수 있다.
debate.against: 고밀도 노선에서는 전철화가 장기적으로 더 싸고 효율적이며, 배터리는 용량·온도·수명 한계가 있다. 배터리만 믿다가 전철화가 늦어지면 장기 목표를 놓칠 수 있다.

roleplay.scenario: You are at a regional transport board meeting deciding how to replace diesel trains on a long, lightly used line. One member wants full electrification; you want a battery-train pilot.
roleplay.your_role: A transport planner arguing for battery trains on the long, lightly used line
roleplay.partner_role: A skeptical board member who favours full electrification and worries about range and cost
goals: Reframe the comparison as battery versus diesel, not battery versus electric
Use at least two expressions such as 'on a case-by-case basis', 'in hindsight' or 'leverage the existing infrastructure'
Acknowledge the range limitation honestly and propose a staged plan

useful_phrases.phrase: To be fair, that depends on the route.
useful_phrases.ko: 공정하게 말하면, 그건 노선에 따라 다르다.

useful_phrases.phrase: For me, the comparison isn't X, it's Y.
useful_phrases.ko: 내 관점에서 비교 대상은 X가 아니라 Y다.

useful_phrases.phrase: Let's look at it on a case-by-case basis.
I can't give you the numbers, but fundamentally...
I can't speak for the wider industry, but from my perspective...
useful_phrases.ko: 업계 전체를 대변할 순 없지만 제 입장에서는...

shadowing.reason_ko: 관용구와 긴 문장 흐름이 섞여 있고, 비교를 이어 가는 자연스러운 리듬과 자기 수정 화법을 연습하기 좋다.
'비교 대상은 A가 아니라 B' 프레임 전환 패턴이 들어 있어 논쟁에서 바로 쓸 수 있다.
'look, we have put the effort in' 같은 단호한 어조와 마무리 문장이 좋아 패널 발언 마무리 연습에 적합하다.

difficulty.note_ko: 철도 기술 용어(traction, rolling stock 등)가 나오지만 문장은 대체로 구어체로 명료하다. 영국식 어휘와 화자의 머뭇거림, 문장을 정정하는 화법이 섞여 있어 C1 수준에서 들을 만하다.

translations_sent.2-2: 뉴스. 저희 Zero에서는 기후 해법 이야기를 많이 해왔지만, 200회가 지나도록 기차 이야기는 한 번도 하지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.3-3: 이번 에피소드가 그 역사적인 실수를 바로잡습니다.
translations_sent.4-4: 기차는 육상 운송 수단 중에서 가장 효율적입니다.
translations_sent.5-5: 디젤 1갤런으로 기차는 1톤의 화물을 500마일 옮길 수 있는데, 대형 트럭은 같은 연료로 그 3분의 1 거리밖에 못 갑니다.
translations_sent.6-6: 그 기차를 친환경 전기로 움직이면, 비할 데 없이 깨끗한 육상 운송 수단이 됩니다.
translations_sent.7-7: 새 철도 노선을 깔고 있는 나라들에게 전기 열차는 이제 고민할 필요도 없는 선택입니다.
translations_sent.8-8: 하지만 영국처럼 전철화 시대 이전에 철도망을 만든 나라들이 많습니다.
translations_sent.9-9: 이런 나라들은 이제 그 노선들을 전철화해야 하는데, 비용도 많이 들고 어려운 일일 수 있습니다.
translations_sent.13-13: 오늘 모실 분은 세계 최대 철도 회사 중 하나인 알스톰의 제품 디렉터, 제임스 오설리번 씨입니다.
translations_sent.14-14: 제임스는 영국에 투입될 배터리 전기 열차 개발을 이끌어 왔습니다.
translations_sent.17-17: 이 프로그램은 기후 해법을 많이 다루는데, 지금까지 기차를 다룬 적은 없었습니다.
translations_sent.18-18: 200회를 하고 나서야 다루게 되어 정말 설렙니다.
translations_sent.19-19: 저는 얼마 전 중국 취재 출장에서 돌아왔는데요.
translations_sent.21-21: 엄청나게 인상적이죠. 아마 세계 최고의 철도망 중 하나일 겁니다.
translations_sent.23-23: 저는 인도에서 자랐는데, 인도 철도망은 그만큼 발전하진 않았지만 꽤 인상적입니다.
translations_sent.24-24: 아주 외진 곳까지, 언덕 위로도 해안가까지도 닿아 있죠.
translations_sent.25-25: 그리고 지금은 거의 전부 전철화되어 있습니다.
translations_sent.26-26: 중국 철도망보다도 전철화 비율이 더 높습니다.
translations_sent.27-27: 하지만 지난 18년 동안 제가 고향이라 부르는 곳은 영국입니다.
translations_sent.28-28: 처음 영국에 왔을 때는 철도망 때문에 과거로 거슬러 올라간 기분이었어요.
translations_sent.29-29: 영국은 가장 빠른 열차도, 가장 앞선 열차도 없고, 사실 전기 열차조차 충분하지 않잖아요.
translations_sent.31-31: 기차를 탄생시킨 나라에서 무엇이 잘못된 걸까요?
translations_sent.32-32: 저는 딱히 뭐가 잘못됐다고 생각하지는 않습니다.
translations_sent.33-33: 다만 백지에서 시작할 수 있었다면 아마 지금과 같은 모습은 아니었을 거라고 말씀드리고 싶네요.
translations_sent.34-34: 영국은 당시에 깔린 빅토리아 시대 인프라의 유산 위에서 살아가고 있다는 점을 기억하셔야 합니다.
translations_sent.35-35: 그 시대 사람들은 최선의 예상과 노력을 다해서 목적에 맞는 것을 설계했던 겁니다.
translations_sent.36-36: 그래서 지금 영국에서 하는 모든 일은, 특히 새 차량을 투입할 때는 레몬에서 마지막 한 방울까지 짜내듯 최대한 최적화하는 것입니다. 인도나 중국과 비교하면요. 인도는 그렇게 최근은 아니지만 영국보다는 더 최근이고요.
translations_sent.37-37: 중국은 인프라를 설치한 시기가 아주 최근이죠.
translations_sent.38-38: 네, 중국은 영국을 보고 배울 수 있었으니까요.
translations_sent.39-39: 그러면 영국이 철도망을 전철화하지 못하게 발목을 잡은 건 무엇일까요?
translations_sent.40-40: 디젤 열차가 증기 열차를 대체하던 시기에는, 디젤이 등장했을 때 증기는 꽤 비효율적이었기 때문에 디젤이 일종의 혁명처럼 여겨졌던 때가 있었다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.41-41: 물론 주말에 시간이 있어서 그 광경을 즐기러 간다면 증기 기관차는 정말 멋지죠.
translations_sent.42-42: 하지만 디젤의 사업성 측면에서 보면, 기관사가 한 명만 있으면 됩니다.
translations_sent.44-44: 승객을 태울 수 있는 훨씬 단순한 동력 분산식 열차를 설계할 수 있었죠.

translations_sent.150-150: 하지만 제가 보기엔 경우마다 다르게 판단해야 합니다.
translations_sent.151-151: 전철화의 어려움 중 하나는 기존 노선에 전철화를 소급 적용하는 거예요.
translations_sent.152-152: 우선, 운행 중인 철도를 방해하면서 공사를 해야 하죠.
translations_sent.153-153: 게다가 현장에 가면 뭐가 나올지 정확히 알 수 없어서 비용이 늘어날 수 있어요.
translations_sent.154-154: 또 하나는 운영 측면인데, 운영사가 이미 운행 중인 서비스에 지장을 주지 않고 공사하려면, 예를 들어 야간이나 휴일 같은 힘든 시간대 작업 때문에 비용이 더 들어요.
translations_sent.155-155: 네. 잠시 후에는 알스톰의 제품 디렉터이자 새로운 세대의 배터리 전기 열차 개발을 돕고 있는 제임스 오설리번과의 대화를 더 들려드리겠습니다.
translations_sent.156-156: 배터리 전기 열차는 열차의 역사에 비하면 꽤 최근에 나온 현상이에요. 일본, 오스트리아, 독일처럼 어떤 형태로든 배터리 전기 열차를 운행해 온 곳들이 있죠.
translations_sent.157-157: 어떤 시장에서 이게 통할 거라고 보시나요?
translations_sent.158-158: 아직 다루지 않았지만 북미를 비롯해 모든 시장에서 등장하는 걸 보고 있어요.
translations_sent.159-159: 그래도 영국은 정말 큰 시장이에요. 오래전에 전기 대신 디젤을 선택했던 유산이 영향을 미치고 있으니까요.
translations_sent.160-160: 그러니까 영국은 전철화 인프라 수준이 예를 들어 독일이나 프랑스만큼 갖춰져 있지 않기 때문에, 전 세계 다른 지역들보다 배터리 열차 시장이 확실히 더 큰 편이죠.
translations_sent.161-161: 배터리 단계에서 멈추고, 전차선까지 굳이 깔 걱정은 하지 않는 세상도 가능할까요?
translations_sent.163-163: 다시 말씀드리지만, 이 계산은 전철화를 얼마나 먼 거리까지 할 건지, 그리고 수송 수요를 맞추려면 열차를 몇 대나 운행하고 싶은지에 달려 있다고 봐요.
translations_sent.164-164: 승객이 많고 이동 거리가 짧다면, 전철화 비용이 상대적으로 저렴할 테니 전철화하는 게 합리적일 가능성이 높아요.
translations_sent.165-165: 배터리 열차로 사야 하는 대수는 많아질 테니 그 비용은 올라가겠죠.
translations_sent.166-166: 그래서 어느 시점에는 완전 전철화로 넘어가는 게 맞을 거예요.
translations_sent.168-168: 승객은 적은데 먼 거리를 운행하는 노선이라면, 배터리 열차를 계속 쓰는 편이 장기적으로 더 저렴할 수 있어요.
translations_sent.169-169: 오늘 어떤 나라에서 철도망을 새로 짓기 시작한다고 해 보죠. 세상에는 제대로 된 철도망을 아직 시작도 못 한 나라가 많잖아요.
translations_sent.170-170: 오늘날의 기술과 그 기술들이 앞으로 갈 수 있는 길을 알고 있다면, 그 철도망은 어떤 모습일까요?
translations_sent.172-172: 처음부터 만든다면 전철화를 하겠죠. 한 번에 다 할 수 있으니까요.
translations_sent.173-173: 부지도 있을 테고, 선로를 까는 동시에 설치하면 되고, 가능한 한 가장 첨단 신호 시스템도 함께 넣을 거예요. 처음 할 때 하는 게 나중에 돌아와서 고치는 것보다 훨씬훨씬 싸니까요.
translations_sent.174-174: 이 Odesia 제품에서는 배터리가 다섯 개 객차에 나뉘어 들어가 있어요.
translations_sent.175-175: 배터리 객차를 열차와 따로 두는 아이디어도 있어요. 배터리로 가야 하는 구간에서만 연결하고, 나머지 구간은 전기로 달리는 거죠.
translations_sent.176-176: 혹시 선생님 회사나 경쟁사 제품 중에 이런 흥미로운 아이디어를 본 적 있나요?
translations_sent.177-177: 열차 전동화를 좀 더 빨리 하려는 시도로요.
translations_sent.178-178: 네. 기관차라는 개념 자체는 수십 년, 아주 오래전부터 있었잖아요.
translations_sent.179-179: 그러니까 일반 전기 열차가 못 하는 일을 해 주는 걸 붙인다는 발상은 새로운 개념이 아니에요.
translations_sent.181-181: 아마 아닐 거예요. 이런 건 계속 반복해서 써야 하는 자산이라는 걸 기억해야 하거든요.
translations_sent.182-182: 하나의 특수한 용도로만 쓰인다면 거기서 얻는 가치가 그다지 크지 않죠.
translations_sent.183-183: 반면 Odessia에 적용한 배터리 열차는 승객 수용량을 최대한으로 살렸어요.
translations_sent.184-184: 저희가 배터리 열차라고 말해 주지 않았다면, 승객 입장에서는 아마 몰랐을 거예요. 내부는 완전히 똑같아 보이니까요.
translations_sent.185-185: 그러니까 수용량이 큰 기존 차량의 장점을 그대로 살리고, 단지 배터리 열차를 만들기 위해 차량을 억지로 변경하지는 않은 거죠.
translations_sent.186-186: 2021년 COP26에서 Alstom은 수소가 영국 철도망의 탈탄소화에 역할을 할 수 있다고 발표했습니다.
translations_sent.187-187: 지난 11월에는 Alstom이 기술이 아직 성숙하지 않았다며 프랑스에서 수소 열차 사업을 중단했고요.
translations_sent.191-191: Odessia Stream만 놓고 보면, 저희는 이른바 '견인 방식에 구애받지 않게' 설계했어요.
translations_sent.192-192: 그러니까 열차가 전기로 달린다는 점을 활용하는 거예요.
translations_sent.193-193: 열차는 전기를 알맞은 속도로 만들어 주기만 하면, 어떤 연료원으로 구동되는지는 신경 쓰지 않아요.
translations_sent.194-194: 그게 디젤이든, 배터리든, 수소든, 아니면 뭐, 미래 어느 시점의 핵융합이든 마찬가지예요.
translations_sent.198-198: 어쨌든 요점은, 어떤 친환경 기술이 등장해서 열차를 움직이게 될지 미래를 예측하는 게 저희 일은 아니라는 거예요.
translations_sent.199-199: 하지만 통합 업체로서 저희가 할 수 있는 건 공간과 인터페이스를 설계하고 거기에 맞게 엔지니어링해 두는 거예요. 그래서 그런 기술이 등장해 매일 승객 운행에 쓸 만큼 충분히 견고해졌을 때 바로 대비가 되어 있게요.
translations_sent.200-200: 그리고 오늘은 이 특정 제품 때문에 영국에 계시지만, 알스톰은 전 세계에 사업을 하고 있잖아요. 가장 빠르게 성장하고 있고, 흥미롭고, 알스톰이 직접 뛰어들어 일하고 있는 시장은 어디인가요?
translations_sent.201-201: 해외로 눈을 돌리기가 아주 쉽긴 한데, 사실 여기 영국에서도 지금이 흥미로운 시기예요.
translations_sent.202-202: 다시 말씀드리지만, 저희가 트랜스페나인에서 따낸 계약의 그 열차들은 정말 참신합니다.
translations_sent.203-203: 저희가 친환경 에너지 쪽에 초점을 맞추긴 하지만, 그 열차들에는 앞으로 달리게 될 노선에서 정말 중요하게 만들어 주는 다른 특징들도 있어요.
translations_sent.204-204: 지속 가능성은 여러 가지 형태로 나타나거든요.
translations_sent.205-205: 친환경 에너지가 하나고, 접근성과 승객 경험, 편안함도 있습니다.
translations_sent.206-206: 이런 모든 요소가 제품에 녹아 있어서 21세기를 위한 열차가 되도록 했고, 이전 세대 철도 차량에서 배운 것을 발전시켰습니다.
translations_sent.207-207: 짚고 넘어갈 만한 또 다른 큰 분야는 디지털화 같은 건데요, 제가 막 베를린에서 열린 세계 최대 철도 박람회인 이노트랜스에서 돌아왔거든요.
translations_sent.208-208: 거기서 저희는 원격 열차 운영을 선보였어요.
translations_sent.209-209: 그러니까 차량기지에서 열차를 원격으로 운전할 수 있는 건데, 열차는 스스로 움직이고 카메라가 전부 설치되어 있는 거죠.
translations_sent.212-212: 열차에서 받는 데이터를 처리하고 개선해서 더 많은 인사이트와 진단, 예측 정비를 얻으려면 AI를 어떻게 활용할까요?
translations_sent.213-213: 그래서 지금 열차 분야에서는 흥미로운 일이 많이 일어나고 있다고 말씀드릴 수 있겠네요.
translations_sent.214-214: 운전 자동화를 생각해 보면, 도로와 자동차는 예측 불가능성이 엄청나게 크고 자동화가 더 복잡한 곳이에요.
translations_sent.215-215: 철도에 예측 불가능성이 전혀 없다는 건 아니지만, 도로보다는 훨씬 낮죠.
translations_sent.216-216: 그리고 물론 자동 운전 열차가 존재해 온 지도 꽤 오래됐고요.
translations_sent.217-217: 여기 런던의 DLR 노선에는 기관사가 없어요.
translations_sent.218-218: 그런데 철도는 자동화하기가 더 단순한데도, 자동화가 활용되는 범위는 제가 생각했던 만큼 넓지 않았어요.
translations_sent.220-220: 철도의 자동화 활용을 보면, 특히 '자동화 등급'이라는 게 있는데, 열차가 얼마나 무인으로 독립적으로 달리느냐에 따라 1단계부터 4단계까지 있어요.
translations_sent.221-221: 전통적인 열차는 GOA1로 운행되는데, 기본적으로 기관사가 있다는 뜻이에요.
translations_sent.222-222: GOA 2는 기관사가 있긴 하지만, 열차가 견인과 제동 쪽을 제어하는 거예요.
translations_sent.223-223: DLR이 해당하는 GOA 3는 꽤 독특한 경우인데, 탑승한 기관사는 없지만 문을 관리하는 승무원은 있어요.
translations_sent.225-225: GOA 3와 4는 대개 아주 폐쇄적인 네트워크에서 운영된다는 걸 알 수 있어요.
translations_sent.227-227: 하지만 간선철도에서는 아직 그 도약을 못 했는데, 간선 열차와 상호작용하는 온갖 요소들 때문이에요. 건널목이나 선로에 접근하는 사람들 같은 것들이죠.
translations_sent.228-228: 늘 문제는 그런 환경에서 어떻게 안전하게 만들 것인가였어요.
translations_sent.229-229: 하지만 그게 바로 이런 열차의 디지털 측면에서 다음 단계입니다.
translations_sent.230-230: 카메라 같은 온보드 센서와 ETCS로의 전환 같은 신호 장비를 사용하면, 간선에서도 그런 자동화 등급의 단계들을 차츰 밟아 나가게 될 거예요.
translations_sent.231-231: 그리고 디지털화의 한 측면으로 제가 짐작하기에 안전 쪽에서 효과가 나타났을 것 같은데요, 항공 인프라에서 그랬던 것처럼요.
translations_sent.232-232: 사고가 점점 줄고 있어요, 사고가 안 일어난다는 말은 아니고요.
translations_sent.233-233: 여기 영국에서도 올해 큰 사고가 하나 있었죠.
translations_sent.234-234: 그런데 디지털화가 안전을 얼마나 빠르게 향상시킬까요?
translations_sent.235-235: 사실 거기엔 어려움이 있다고 생각해요. 디지털화는 엄청나게 빠른 속도로 움직이는데, 안전한 시스템을 유지하려면 더 느리고 더 체계적인 접근이 필요하거든요.
translations_sent.236-236: 저희가 안전 시스템에 접근하는 방식을 보면, 어떤 일이 일어날 확률을 사실상 0으로 줄이는 것이 핵심이에요.
translations_sent.237-237: 그러니까 치명적인 사고 중 일부는 확률이 너무 낮아서, 열차 편성이 꾸준히 운행되는 수명 동안에는 일어나지 않아야 한다는 거죠.
translations_sent.238-238: 그렇다면 디지털 측면에서는, 예를 들어 소프트웨어로 제어되는 열차가 안전하도록 기능을 매번 똑같이, 반복 가능하고 신뢰할 수 있게 수행하게 하려면 어떻게 해야 하느냐가 문제예요.
translations_sent.239-239: AI가 소프트웨어를 만들고 코드를 쓰는 방식을 생각해 보면, 반복 가능한 편이 아니에요.
translations_sent.240-240: 그러니까 그 두 가지는 서로 별개의 문제라고 할 수 있죠.
translations_sent.241-241: 그래서 우리 업계가 그걸 꺼리거나 피하는 건 아니지만, 분명 도전 과제이긴 합니다.
translations_sent.242-242: 영국 철도망에 지금이 흥미로운 시기일 수 있다고 말씀하셨죠.
translations_sent.243-243: 영국 철도의 재건은 계속해서 반복적으로 나온 프로젝트입니다.
translations_sent.245-245: 가장 최근의 것은 철도망을 실제로 국유화하는 건데, 정부가 지난 몇 년간 추진해 온 일이죠.
translations_sent.246-246: 이번에도 또 하나의 헛된 새벽이 될까 봐 걱정되지는 않으신가요?
translations_sent.247-247: 그리고 그렇지 않다면, 이번에는 철도망을 다시 만들고, 전철화하고, 친환경으로 바꾸는 이 재건이 빠른 속도로 계속될 거라고 확신하시는 이유가 뭔가요?
translations_sent.248-248: 업계 전체를 대변할 수는 없지만, 개인적으로나 알스톰의 입장에서 보면 이 프로젝트는 업계나 우리 제품뿐 아니라 그 일에 참여한 엔지니어들, 즉 사람들의 역량을 보여줄 기회를 준다고 생각합니다. 영국 철도 시장에 제품을 공급할 기회가 주어지면 해낼 수 있다는 걸 분명히 강조할 수 있죠.
translations_sent.249-249: 실제로 우리는 그걸 바탕으로 새로운 제품들을 선보이고, 승객들에게 혜택을 주고, 기술을 더 친환경적으로 만들고, 지속 가능성을 높일 수 있습니다.
